lines: 1 existing; 0 proposed structure(s). Selected enterprise: honey. No animal head count or output is assumed.
Buying advice: match breed/stock to the product, local feed, climate and care capacity; confirm with a local livestock or beekeeping adviser.
Harvest depends on the colony, local flowering and rainfall. Inspect ripeness and leave food for the colony; there is no fixed national honey season.
Time to first product: not sourced for this enterprise.

Production reference: 25 kg honey/hive/year. From a 2008 national postal survey of 112 SABIO-member beekeepers (22.4% response rate) managing an estimated 19,520 hives at 2,094 apiary sites; figure is self-reported and un-weighted. Table 7 (same doc, p.13-14) shows wide variance by region/operation-focus/size for the same year: e.g. 'All' region, honey-focused, all-size operations = 25.1-26.9 kg/hive/yr across 3 survey sites; Western Cape honey-focused = 23.6-27.9 kg/hive/yr; Western Cape pollination-focused, small operations = only 7.0-7.5 kg/hive/yr. The same document also quotes an earlier, more rigorously validated study: 'Their average reported yield is very low, at just 13.4 kilograms per hive' for Western Cape hives (Allsopp & Cherry 2004, cited p.2 of this working paper), and historical national bee-census data of 8.3 kg/hive/annum (1911-1988 average) rising to 24 kg/hive in the 1974/5 census (same doc, p.1). No single number can be called definitive; 25 kg/hive/yr is used as the document's own headline national estimate.
Check the detailed enterprise references for feed and housing. Match the ration and space to the animal stage and housing system; provide dependable clean water.
Keep hives away from playgrounds, provide fresh water and use a dry site. Ask a registered beekeeper to check safe local placement before adding a hive.
Inspect every colony regularly for signs of notifiable bee disease and Cape-bee (Capensis) infection.
Site and secure hives against theft and vandalism, which is one of the biggest challenges facing South African beekeepers.
Register with the Department before beekeeping. Registration lasts 24 months from registration or renewal and must be renewed when it expires.
A beekeeper who fails to renew registration at expiry will be deregistered and face penalties under the Act.
Beekeeping activities and hired beekeeping services require a valid registration certificate. Check the certificate before using a beekeeper.
Every beehive must be clearly and legibly marked with the beekeeper's registration number.
Keep written records of colonies, apiary locations, diseases, disease-control measures and colony losses with their reasons.
Do not move honeybees across the Cape bee line, or keep Cape bees north of it, without written approval.
Report any suspected notifiable disease (American foulbrood is listed); officials can order an infected colony destroyed.

lines: 1 existing; 0 proposed structure(s). Selected enterprise: meat. No animal head count or output is assumed.
Buying advice: match breed/stock to the product, local feed, climate and care capacity; confirm with a local livestock or beekeeping adviser.
Time to first product: not sourced for this enterprise.

Production reference: 114.5–121.2 kg weaning weight/calf. Table 5 gives weaning weight (WW) across four agro-ecological zones for the same nine Nguni communal herds: arid 114.51 kg (lowest), semi-arid 119.98 kg, dry sub-humid 117.91 kg, humid 121.21 kg (highest). The range recorded here spans this one study's own arid-to-humid zone means; it is not merged with any other paper's weaning-weight figures (other SA studies report different ranges for different systems - e.g. research-station or stud herds - and were deliberately excluded to avoid mixing systems). 826 Nguni calves from nine herds that the paper itself says were 'kept under extensive grazing system' in Limpopo Province - a genuine communal/extensive veld system matching this enterprise.

Productive-life reference: 6.4 years. 2354 days / 365.25 = 6.44 years. 'Failure time' is the length of productive herd life for the 580 uncensored (fully-observed) records in the combined dataset; the dissertation itself defines productive herd life as 'the time interval between first calving date to culling date'. Combined data from three extensively-grazed Nguni stud herds, animals born 1968-2015.
Check the detailed enterprise references for feed and housing. Match the ration and space to the animal stage and housing system; provide dependable clean water.
Cattle pens must not be overcrowded: there must be enough floor space for every animal to lie down at the same time.
During transport, cattle must have at least 1.4 m² of floor space each so loading is neither too tight nor too loose.
Cattle may not be transported for more than 18 hours without being off-loaded and given feed, water and shelter.
It is an offence to starve, under-feed, or deny water or food to cattle.
Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) is a controlled animal disease under the Animal Diseases Act: state Veterinary Services enforce isolation and movement restrictions.
Every cattle owner must register an official identification mark and brand or mark their cattle with it, under the Animal Identification Act.

Any suspected or confirmed brucellosis-related abortion in cattle must be reported to the State Veterinary office, as part of the national bovine brucellosis control scheme under the Animal Diseases Act.
No animal may be slaughtered anywhere but a registered abattoir, with the exception below.
Slaughter for the farmer's own household consumption, or for cultural or religious purposes, is exempt from the abattoir rule.

animalProducts.title: Chickens: Broilers (commercial)
lines: 1 existing; 0 proposed structure(s). Selected enterprise: meat. No animal head count or output is assumed.
Buying advice: choose a meat strain and supplier batch plan; confirm brooding, feed, water and slaughter arrangements.
Plan balanced feed, clean water, shade, ventilation and predator protection. Egg supply depends on laying birds, their age, health and care; a coop alone supplies no eggs.

First product reference: 4.6–4.7 weeks. 32 days / 7 = 4.57 weeks; 33 days / 7 = 4.71 weeks. This enterprise has a single grow-out cycle ending in slaughter, so 'time to first product' = age at slaughter. South Africa, commercial industry average.

Production reference: 1.8–1.9 kg/bird at slaughter (32–33 days). National commercial broiler industry average, South Africa, 2022. A separate breed-trial table (Table 4b, same document, p.39) gives named-strain 'Cumulative FI (kg)' and 'Body weight (kg)' at exactly 35 days: Arbor Acres Plus 2.29kg, Cobb 500 2.52kg, Indian River 2.30kg, Ross 308 2.30kg (cumulative feed intake 3.21-3.64kg) - a slightly older age (35 vs 32-33 days) and higher weight than the industry-wide average quoted above; not merged into the primary figure since it is a different (breed-standard trial) dataset, but used below for the feed-intake figure.

Age/system reference: Newer South African commercial reference: SAPA 2024 reports average slaughter at 30–31 days with bird weight 1.8–1.85 kg. The primary range above remains the earlier 2022 reference at 32–33 days. These are commercial bird weights, not dressed meat kg or a village flock target. Record hatch or purchase age, feeding system, actual harvest date and weighed product basis.
Check the detailed enterprise references for feed and housing. Match the ration and space to the animal stage and housing system; provide dependable clean water.
Floor-housed broilers: no more than 40 kg of bird per square metre.
Newly hatched chicks must be given feed within 24 hours of hatching.
Newly hatched chicks must be given access to water within 24 hours of hatching, sooner in hot weather.
Fresh water and the right feed always available, so birds are free from hunger and thirst.
Broiler houses need a minimum ventilation/airflow rate of 5 cubic metres per hour for every kilogram of bird mass in the house.
In free-range broiler production, indoor stocking must not exceed 15 birds per square metre of floor space.
An owner or manager whose animals are, or may be, infected with a controlled animal disease must report it to the state veterinary director immediately.
Newcastle disease and notifiable avian influenza are on the state list of controlled and notifiable animal diseases.
No animal may be slaughtered anywhere but an abattoir, with the exceptions below.
Slaughter for your own household, or for cultural or religious purposes, is exempt from the abattoir rule.

lines: 1 existing; 0 proposed structure(s). Selected enterprise: eggs. No animal head count or output is assumed.
Buying advice: Potchefstroom Koekoek is a dual-purpose option; Venda, Ovambo and Naked Neck are other ARC-conserved options. No province-specific winning breed is claimed.
Plan balanced feed, clean water, shade, ventilation and predator protection. Egg supply depends on laying birds, their age, health and care; a coop alone supplies no eggs.
Collect eggs frequently, keep nest litter clean and dry, and handle/store eggs carefully for household use or sale.

First product reference: 15.7–27.8 weeks. Free-range village chickens, KwaZulu-Natal; dry-environment birds started laying earlier (15.74 weeks) than wet-environment birds (27.78 weeks), difference flagged significant ('*') in the source table. Wide range reflects genuine dry/wet-season environmental variation reported by the source, not measurement uncertainty.

Production reference: 40.4–49.9 eggs/hen/year. Free-range/scavenging village chickens, KwaZulu-Natal: dry (40.43) vs wet (49.91) environment, difference not significant ('NS'). A managed-system ARC Irene trial of named indigenous breeds (Grobbelaar, Sutherland & Molalakgotla 2010, Animal Genetic Resources 46: 25-32) reports far higher counts, now separately verified and retained in productionReferences; managed conditions cannot replace this village range.

Age/system reference: The ARC Irene trial compared Potchefstroom Koekoek, Venda, Ovambo and Naked Neck under commercial feed, water and controlled lighting. Mean eggs/hen in a 52-week cycle were 195.9, 153.7, 125.5 and 138.9 respectively; first-egg ages were 138.5, 139.0, 134.5 and 129.0 days from hatch, with no significant first-egg age difference among breeds. This is managed breed context, not the yield of scavenging hens in KZN. Match feeding and housing before using a benchmark.
Check the detailed enterprise references for feed and housing. Match the ration and space to the animal stage and housing system; provide dependable clean water.
In extensive village systems the chickens have to find their own water and food.
Scavenging village chickens grow more slowly than commercially-farmed birds and are more vulnerable to disease, parasites and predators.
In the Limpopo and KwaZulu-Natal survey, 94.9% of farmers housed their chickens at night.
What free-ranging hens forage met their needs for maintenance and growth but not for laying: protein in every season, calcium and phosphorus in winter.

lines: 1 existing; 0 proposed structure(s). Selected enterprise: eggs. No animal head count or output is assumed.
Buying advice: for egg production, request vaccinated point-of-lay pullets from a layer supplier, with age, feeding and vaccination records.
Plan balanced feed, clean water, shade, ventilation and predator protection. Egg supply depends on laying birds, their age, health and care; a coop alone supplies no eggs.
Collect eggs frequently, keep nest litter clean and dry, and handle/store eggs carefully for household use or sale.
Season reference: With a constant 14–16 hour light day, commercial hens keep laying at a high rate all year. This commercial management reference is not a naturally flat household egg supply.
First product reference: 21 weeks. Bird age from hatch; confirm the strain and rearing with the supplier. Point-of-lay birds start later in this cycle.

Table 4a's cumulative 'Eggs/hen housed' for five commercial strains; the same table gives 'Age at depop. weeks 90.0' for every strain. Check the detailed enterprise references for feed and housing. Match the ration and space to the animal stage and housing system; provide dependable clean water.
In free-range systems, hens must have access to the outdoor range for at least 8 hours a day in daylight.
Where individual nest boxes are used, at least one nest for every 8 hens.
Hens need at least 8 hours of continuous darkness in every 24-hour cycle to rest properly.
Floor housing needs litter on at least a third (33%) of the floor.
The outdoor free-range area must not be overstocked: no more than 5 birds per square metre of range.
An owner or manager whose animals are, or may be, infected with a controlled animal disease must report it to the state veterinary director immediately.
Newcastle disease and notifiable avian influenza are on the state list of controlled and notifiable animal diseases.
No animal may be slaughtered anywhere but an abattoir, with the exceptions below.
Slaughter for your own household, or for cultural or religious purposes, is exempt from the abattoir rule.

cases.name: enterprise-duck

animalProducts.title: Ducks: Meat duck (Pekin / Muscovy, backyard)
lines: 1 existing; 0 proposed structure(s). Selected enterprise: meat. No animal head count or output is assumed.
Buying advice: match breed/stock to the product, local feed, climate and care capacity; confirm with a local livestock or beekeeping adviser.

First product reference: 7–12 weeks. P44 = Pekin (7 weeks to slaughter); MR71 = Muscovy (10 weeks for ducks/hens, 12 weeks for drakes). Treated as 'time to first product' = age to slaughter, since this is a single-cycle meat enterprise (no repeat product like eggs). Non-South-African trial by Warsaw researchers, published in SAJAS; journal location does not establish local applicability.

Production reference: 2.3–2.9 kg live weight/bird at slaughter. Non-SA (Guyana study reporting a citation to Steklenev 1990); no SA-specific absolute slaughter live-weight figure was found (see gaps). 2.93 kg = Pekin at 8-10 weeks, 2.29 kg = Muscovy at 8-10 weeks - matches this enterprise's two breeds. The same LRRD paper's own experiment (Table 2, intensive system, Guyana) measured live weight at slaughter (8 weeks) as: Pekin drakes 2.53 kg, Pekin hens 2.29 kg, Muscovy drakes 2.47 kg, Muscovy hens 1.51 kg - broadly consistent with, but not merged into, the cited range above since it is a separate dataset/table in the same source. No sourced eggs/duck/year figure was found for either breed (see gaps); the LRRD and SAJAS sources used here studied ducks reared only for meat.
Check the detailed enterprise references for feed and housing. Match the ration and space to the animal stage and housing system; provide dependable clean water.
It is an offence to deny a duck food or water, or keep it somewhere lacking adequate space, ventilation, light or shelter from heat and cold.
Watch flocks for sudden deaths, ruffled feathers, swollen wattles/combs or a sudden drop in egg production - these are signs of avian influenza and should be reported at once.
Keep ducks away from wild birds and open water/feed that attracts them, and control visitors' access to duck housing, to reduce avian-influenza risk.
Ducks are one of the domesticated animal species listed in the Meat Safety Act, so its rules on registered abattoirs and hygiene apply to them.
Ducks slaughtered to be sold must be slaughtered at a registered abattoir; slaughter for the farmer's own consumption is exempt but that meat may not be sold.
At the abattoir, ducks must be handled humanely during loading, transport, offloading, housing, immobilising and killing, under the Animals Protection Act.
Ducks are birds/poultry, so an outbreak of avian influenza in a duck flock is a controlled animal disease under the Animal Diseases Act and must be reported to the state vet immediately.

cases.name: enterprise-fish-tilapia

animalProducts.title: Pond: Tilapia (Mozambique tilapia, small pond or tank)
lines: 1 existing; 0 proposed structure(s). Selected enterprise: fish. No animal head count or output is assumed.
Buying advice: match breed/stock to the product, local feed, climate and care capacity; confirm with a local livestock or beekeeping adviser.

First product reference: 43.5–52.2 weeks. 10 months x 4.35 = 43.5 weeks; 12 months x 4.35 = 52.2 weeks. This is Mozambique Tilapia (O. mossambicus) grow-out time to harvestable size; the source separately states Nile Tilapia (O. niloticus) reaches harvestable maturity faster, in 6-10 months (= 26.1-43.5 weeks) — not used here as it is a different species with a different legal status (see 'legal').

Production reference: 800 g harvest weight/fish. Table 8-3 gives the Mozambique Tilapia's harvestable size as an approximate single figure ('+- 800g'), not a range, so [800, 800] is used rather than inventing a spread. The same table cell wraps '10-12' across a line break in the PDF ('10-\n12'), kept verbatim. The table's Nile Tilapia row gives the same approximate weight (+-800g) reached faster, in 6-10 months — not used here because this dossier is framed around the indigenous, legally unrestricted Mozambique Tilapia per task instruction; see 'legal' for why Nile Tilapia is treated separately. No SA source was found giving a feed-conversion-based or per-hectare yield figure specific to O. mossambicus that could be converted to this per-fish unit without stitching numbers across documents, so outputUnit follows the source's own unit (grams harvest weight per fish) rather than being converted.

Age/system reference: ARC makes tilapia suitability depend on water temperature: summer grow-out can be suitable anywhere in South Africa when water exceeds 20°C; growth is poor below 18°C and winter water below 13°C can kill farmed tilapia. The Highveld reference is a summer crop; tunnels can widen the range. Measure pond water and confirm stocking species and dates. Air climate or a mapped pond does not prove harvest months, fish numbers or food kg.
Check the detailed enterprise references for feed and housing. Match the ration and space to the animal stage and housing system; provide dependable clean water.
The indigenous Mozambique Tilapia (O. mossambicus) is not a listed invasive species and may be farmed without an alien-species permit; the faster-growing Nile Tilapia (O. niloticus) is.

Nile Tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) is a nationally listed invasive fish species: Category 1b inside National Parks, Provincial Reserves, Mountain Catchment Areas and Forestry Reserves, and Category 3 in all other areas.
Outside protected areas Nile tilapia is Category 3: it may remain in prescribed areas or provinces, but further propagation or trade is prohibited.
Nile Tilapia has been listed under the NEMBA Alien and Invasive Species Regulations as requiring a permit to produce.
Producing an alien or invasive species (such as Nile Tilapia) is prohibited in areas designated under the Protected Areas Act and the Fish Sanctuary Act; a permit is required to produce it elsewhere.
Producing tilapia in South Africa requires a water use licence under the National Water Act.

animalProducts.title: Goats: Dairy goat (Saanen / Toggenburg / British Alpine)
lines: 1 existing; 0 proposed structure(s). Selected enterprise: milk. No animal head count or output is assumed.
Buying advice: match breed/stock to the product, local feed, climate and care capacity; confirm with a local livestock or beekeeping adviser.
Plan around actual calving/kidding and lactation. Dry animals do not supply milk.
Time to first product: not sourced for this enterprise.

Production reference: 775.4–1073.4 kg milk/doe/305-day lactation. Lowest (≥7th parity) and highest (3rd parity) group means for milk yield per 305-day standardised lactation in 16,407 analysed South African ARC Saanen lactation records, 1955–2018, mostly intensive/semi-intensive stud herds. Original PDF Table 3 labels the last group ≥7th; HTML renders it >7th. Kept in kg, without litres conversion, annualisation or yield-by-age interpolation.

Age/system reference: South African Saanen reference by lactation number, not age in years: mean milk mass per standardised 305-day lactation was 947.3 kg at first parity, 1043.2 at second, 1073.4 at third, 1020.3 at fourth, 972.8 at fifth, 901.6 at sixth and 775.4 at ≥7th. These ARC milk-recorded groups were mostly intensive/semi-intensive stud herds. Record actual kidding date, lactation number and collected milk; do not divide these totals evenly into months.

Age/system reference: At Putukwane near Polokwane, 179 lactating does under extensive feeding with irregular supplementation were observed for 210 days after kidding. Mean milk mass was 1.45 kg/day for Saanen, 0.75 for British Alpine and 0.56 for Toggenburg during observed lactation. Early lactation exceeded mid and late lactation; March–April kidding outperformed October–November in this cohort. These conditions differ from stud-herd records. Age/system reference: ARC Table 1 lists pregnant sows at 10–18 L drinking water/day and lactating sows at 18–23 L/day. These are breeding-sow stages, not one amount for every pig. Farrowing care separates sow cooling from piglet warmth; outdoor systems need locally adapted hardy stock, shade and shelter. Confirm stage, reliable clean water, feed and housing locally. In heat waves, pig houses need better ventilation/airflow and lower stocking density, and outdoor pigs need shade and shelter.
African swine fever (ASF) is listed as a controlled animal disease pertaining to pigs under the Animal Diseases Act; warthogs and Ornithodorus ticks are carriers/vectors.
Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) is also listed as a controlled animal disease pertaining to pigs under the Animal Diseases Act.
Swill (food waste) may not be fed to pigs unless it has been boiled for at least 60 minutes or sterilised by another equally effective method.
Pigs may only be moved into a biosecure compartment from another compartment that is officially certified/approved for that purpose.
A pig may not be slaughtered anywhere but a registered abattoir, except for own household consumption or cultural/religious purposes.
A pig owner must apply to register an official identification mark and mark their pigs with it, under the Animal Identification Act.

animalProducts.title: Kraal: Meat sheep (Dorper, Damara, indigenous fat-tailed and crossbred)
lines: 1 existing; 0 proposed structure(s). Selected enterprise: meat. No animal head count or output is assumed.
Buying advice: match breed/stock to the product, local feed, climate and care capacity; confirm with a local livestock or beekeeping adviser.
Time to first product: not sourced for this enterprise.

Production reference: 0.6–1.4 lambs born per ewe. outputUnit is 'lambs born/ewe/year' rather than the suggested 'kg live weight/lamb at weaning or slaughter' or 'lambs weaned/ewe/year': the source explains 'Measuring accurate lambing percentages for smallholder sheep farmers is challenging as these farmers mostly farm extensively and do not keep records', and instead calculates 'Lambs born per ewe (as recorded from the surveys based on interviews with individual respondents)' - a lambing (born), not weaning, figure, self-reported by smallholder farmers rather than measured/weighed. 139%=1.39, 83%=0.83, 61%=0.61 lambs born/ewe/year; the range [0.61, 1.39] spans the three Western Cape smallholder districts surveyed (Eden, Central Karoo, West Coast), all from this one study/quote - not merged with any other document. The same paper separately states a COMMERCIAL extensive benchmark of 110-156% lambing and 94-132% weaning (Snyman & Herselman, 2005), explicitly 'expressed over ewes joined' (a different denominator/system) - not merged into this smallholder range.

Age/system reference: The government sheep manual describes controlled breeding at Mara Research Station, Limpopo: June–July mating and November–December lambing to match rain and grass. This is one station breeding calendar, not mutton harvest months. Match adapted meat-purpose stock and feed locally, then record birth, survival, weaning and actual slaughter or sale; lambs born per ewe are not edible kg.
Check the detailed enterprise references for feed and housing. Match the ration and space to the animal stage and housing system; provide dependable clean water.
Sheep must not be penned overcrowded: at least 0.56 square metres of floor space per sheep so every animal can lie down.
Electric prodders, sticks or goads may not be used on sheep.
Sheep driven on the hoof may not be moved more than 20 km in a single day (25 km is regarded as excessive).
Livestock must be given water and fed as soon as they reach their night camp or final destination.
Injured, disabled or blind sheep must be given priority slaughter, or emergency slaughter, to prevent further pain or distress.
Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) is a controlled animal disease under the Animal Diseases Act; Veterinary Services enforce isolation and movement restrictions.
Inside a declared FMD zone, sheep and their products cannot be moved into, out of, or within it without a state veterinary permit.
Sheep scab is a controlled disease by law: a suspected or positive case must be reported to the State Veterinarian immediately.
Against sheep scab, all small stock on the farm must be treated with a remedy registered under Act 36 of 1947, and infected sheep treated twice, eight to ten days apart.
Every sheep owner must register an official identification mark and mark their sheep with it, under the Animal Identification Act.
A sheep may be slaughtered only at an abattoir, except for the farmer's own consumption or for cultural or religious purposes.

animalProducts.title: Kraal: Wool sheep (Merino / Dohne Merino, incl. communal wool growers)
lines: 1 existing; 0 proposed structure(s). Selected enterprise: wool (non-food). No animal head count or output is assumed.
Buying advice: match breed/stock to the product, local feed, climate and care capacity; confirm with a local livestock or beekeeping adviser.
Time to first product: not sourced for this enterprise.

Production reference: 4–5 kg greasy wool/sheep/year. Semi-arid/extensive-veld range (4-5 kg greasy wool/sheep/year) used as the primary value; the same sentence's 8 kg/year figure is for a different system (sheep grazing CULTIVATED pastures) and is deliberately excluded from the range rather than averaged in. A Western Cape Government (Elsenburg) Dohne Merino Extensive enterprise budget (Ceres-Karoo, 2024) separately reports total flock wool sold as 4439.64 kg from a flock of '1 519' Smallstock Units, i.e. 4439.64/1519 = 2.92 kg per Smallstock Unit/year - not used as the primary value because the source does not state that 1 Smallstock Unit = 1 sheep (SSU is a standardised stock-class weighting, not a literal head count), so converting it to kg/sheep would require an unstated conversion factor. A separate NWGA/Mandela Initiative paper on the Eastern Cape communal Wool Sheep Development Program reports a Grootfontein ADI progeny-test 'Greasy fleece weight (kg) 2.8 [commercial rams] 2.4 [communal rams]' for communal Eastern Cape flocks - not merged into the primary value because that table is explicitly for '6-month old lambs' (a different life stage from a mature sheep's full annual clip), consistent with the rule against mixing figures across life stages; kept here only as EC-communal context: commercial-ram-sired lambs at 6 months averaged 2.8 kg, communal-ram-sired lambs 2.4 kg, a +16% difference.
Check the detailed enterprise references for feed and housing. Match the ration and space to the animal stage and housing system; provide dependable clean water.
Sheep must not be penned overcrowded: at least 0.56 square metres of floor space per sheep so every animal can lie down.
Electric prodders, sticks or goads may not be used on sheep.
Sheep driven on the hoof may not be moved more than 20 km in a single day (25 km is regarded as excessive).
Injured, disabled or blind sheep must be given priority slaughter, or emergency slaughter, to prevent further pain or distress.
A sheep-scab treatment plan should be in place: the disease carries a high economic and welfare cost.
Despite foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) in South Africa, wool exports continue under the inactivation clause of the OIE (World Organisation for Animal Health) rules.
Inside a declared FMD zone, sheep and their products cannot be moved into, out of, or within it without a state veterinary permit.
Sheep scab is a controlled disease by law: a suspected or positive case must be reported to the State Veterinarian immediately.
Wool from scab-infected sheep must be destroyed rather than sent to the buyer, where it would be marked as scab wool.
Every sheep owner must register an official identification mark and mark their sheep with it, under the Animal Identification Act.
A sheep may be slaughtered only at an abattoir, except for the farmer's own consumption or for cultural or religious purposes.
